entry.title: 🚗 The Hidden Psychology of Why People Hold Onto Old Cars (and How Tech Helps Them Let Go)
entry.summary: Ever walked past your old car in the driveway and felt guilty, even though it hasn’t moved in 2 years? We tell ourselves: “Maybe I’ll fix it one day” or “It has too many memories to let go.” But behind these excuses lies something deeper: human psychology. And surprisingly, technology is starting to help people overcome it. 🧠 Why We Get Emotionally Attached to Cars Cars aren’t just metal and wheels — they’re symbols of freedom, milestones, and identity. Your first road trip. The car you drove to your first job. The one that carried your family around for years. This emotional connection makes it hard to let go. Psychologists call this loss aversion — we’d rather hold onto something useless than face the feeling of loss. 💸 The Hidden Cost of Keeping an Unwanted Car But here’s the thing: while we cling to old cars emotionally, they’re silently costing us: Insurance premiums for a vehicle we don’t drive. Parking space that could be used better. Safety risks as rust and mechanical failures pile up. When you add it all up, holding onto that car isn’t nostalgia — it’s financial and emotional baggage. ⚙️ How Tech Makes Letting Go Easier This is where technology steps in. Instant online quotes so you know the car’s worth without awkward negotiations. Optimized pickup scheduling so you don’t waste time waiting. Paperwork automation so you don’t drown in forms. By removing barriers, tech makes the decision feel less painful — it’s no longer about “losing” your car, but about “gaining” freedom and cash. 💬 Your Turn Letting go of an old car is really just a metaphor for letting go of anything we cling to: unused gadgets, outdated code we’re too proud to delete, or even projects we know won’t scale. 👉 What’s the hardest thing you’ve ever struggled to let go of — and what finally made you do it? Share your story in the comments 👇 — your insight might just help someone else finally move on. 🔗 If you’re in Australia and looking for a stress-free way to say goodbye to your old car, check out CashForUnwantedCarRemoval .

entry.title: JavaScript Quick Tips
Why Investing Only in Bitcoin Makes Sense
entry.summary: Investing in Bitcoin makes sense for several key reasons. Unlike many altcoins that offer various improvements and features, Bitcoin remains the main player in the cryptocurrency market. Advantages of Bitcoin Lightning Network: Bitcoin has long addressed the issue of high fees through the Lightning Network. This technology allows for transactions with minimal fees and high speed, making it more convenient for users. Low Fees: Even in Bitcoin's main network, fees remain minimal today, making it attractive for investors and users. Stability and Security: The Bitcoin blockchain is the most secure and time-tested. Altcoins often have vulnerabilities that can lead to losses for investors. Ecosystem Development: A multitude of useful applications and services are being developed on the Bitcoin platform, confirming its viability and relevance. Resource Concentration: Many developers spend time creating projects on less secure blockchains, while all necessary functions are already implemented in Bitcoin. This distracts from the main focus—developing and improving the Bitcoin network. The Future of Altcoins Considering all the above factors, it can be assumed that the only way for altcoin projects will be to integrate their systems onto the Bitcoin blockchain. This will allow them to focus on developing their applications without worrying about security. I have concluded that only the Bitcoin blockchain can meet all the needs of users and investors. The ecosystem that exists on its basis is impressive and demonstrates that Bitcoin remains the leader in the world of cryptocurrencies.

entry.title: hurl
entry.summary:
Why I Use Hurl for HTTP API Testing
As a developer who often tests and experiments with APIs, I’m always on the lookout for simple yet powerful tools. Recently, I started using Hurl, and it’s quickly become one of my favorites for running and testing HTTP requests. Hurl lets me write HTTP requests in plain text files, exactly how I would type them in a terminal or Postman, but with the added ability to automate sequences and handle variables. This means I can chain requests, grab OAuth tokens from one response, and use them in the next request — all without writing complicated scripts in another language. It’s a command-line tool, which fits perfectly into my workflow and CI/CD pipelines. I appreciate that it’s lightweight, fast, and supports modern features like HTTP/2 and retries. The syntax is straightforward, so there’s almost no learning curve. Here’s a simple GET request I’ve used to fetch user data: GET https://api.example.com/users Accept: application/json
HTTP/1.1 200 [Asserts] jsonpath "$.length()" > 0
And here’s how I retrieve an OAuth token and use it in another request: POST https://auth.example.com/oauth/token Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
grant_type=client_credentials&client_id=YOUR_ID&client_secret=YOUR_SECRET
HTTP/1.1 200 jsonpath "$.access_token" != null [Capture] token = jsonpath("$.access_token")
GET https://api.example.com/data Authorization: Bearer {{token}}
HTTP/1.1 200
If you want to try it out, installing Hurl is easy with Homebrew: brew install hurl
For more details and documentation, check out the official site: https://hurl.dev/ Hurl has simplified my API testing and automation work dramatically. If you want a no-fuss, scriptable way to run HTTP requests and manage OAuth tokens, give it a try — it might just save you a lot of time.
